narratives.Overview:
> **Recut 2026-08-28** to the bound contract in successor lean `5448167030`, synthesis accepted `5448179517`. The original filing diagnosed this as clause over-derivation by volume and proposed capping or validating what derivation emits. A three-critic panel refuted the remedy, the contrary, the trigger, and the central measurement. History is in the thread.

## Summary

Clause derivation fell through to a **last-resort branch** and transcribed 58 path-bearing lines out of an issue's analysis thread, while a clean 13-clause acceptance surface sat in the same brief where the extractor could not see it. The resulting brief fails `verify:ac` and therefore cannot be committed, so it lives only on one machine while its issue stays open.

The volume is a symptom of branch selection. It is not the defect.

## Measured

**The trigger is branch fall-through.** All 58 clauses came from `collectPathBearingLines`, which runs only when the three primary extractors return zero — and on #3794 all three did. Across 110 derived-clause briefs: primary extractors n=44, max 13; fallback n=66, ceiling at least 75. Every count above 13 in the corpus came from the fallback.

**13 is a branch ceiling, not a norm.** The primary branch transcribes an author-written acceptance list, so the low counts are not under-derivation.

**The acceptance surface was already present and unreadable.** All 13 `plan.items` on #3794 carry empty `narrative` objects; their criteria live in `item.title`, which `collectTaskStatementFromPlan` never reads. Derivation scraped 84,535 characters of issue thread instead. Zero of those 13 criteria appear anywhere in the 58 clauses.

**`verify:ac` passes on `failed === 0 AND (verified > 0 OR clauses === 0)`.** The second conjunct is load-bearing and is currently satisfied by a false positive: an absent artifact returns `verified` with "artifact correctly absent," and on the live brief the single passing clause is a bare `git.ts` that does not exist, matched against the words "does not exist" in analysis prose.

**Every remedy the original filing proposed leaves the brief uncommittable.** Cap at 13, drop non-resolving `artifact_path` at derivation, strip line-range suffixes, and reclassify unresolvable paths as advisory were each executed as counterfactuals against the live brief. All five land `ok = false`.

## Bound remedy

1. **Read `item.title` when `narrative` is empty.** This is the fix that would have prevented the incident outright — the acceptance surface existed and the extractor could not reach it.
2. **Fix the `ok` predicate's `verified > 0` conjunct.** No remedy that leaves it untouched makes the brief committable, and it is currently propped up by an absent-file false positive.
3. **Treat the durability failure as the primary harm.** An uncommittable brief is untracked repository state on a single machine, which is the loss this issue exists to prevent.

⊗ Do not cap clause volume. No valid baseline, wrong mechanism, and it hands a third-party commenter a switch: padding a thread with path-shaped tokens can push an issue past the threshold to block ingest or silently suppress its acceptance surface.

⊗ Do not validate `artifact_path` existence at derivation. Temporally unsound — the artifact is what the work will create.

⊗ Do not reclassify unresolvable paths as advisory. Unsafe, and it does not make the brief committable.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Derivation reads `item.title` when `narrative` is empty, and prefers a present `plan.items` acceptance surface over thread scraping
- [ ] The #3794 brief derives a clause set that passes `verify:ac` and can be committed
- [ ] An absent artifact no longer yields `verified` on prose alone
- [ ] The `ok` predicate does not pass on a false-positive `verified`
- [ ] No clause-count cap is introduced
- [ ] Regression pins the #3794 shape: three primary extractors returning zero must not silently produce a thread-scraped surface
- [ ] Existing briefs are not retroactively invalidated
- [ ] CHANGELOG `[Unreleased]` entry

## Out of scope

- **#3835** — `verify:ac` reading an in-root file named by untrusted prose and matching needles from that same prose. Surfaced by this panel, different remedy, filed separately.
- #3828, the D12 stale-origin gate, which hit the same brief.
- Whether the fallback branch should be removed outright rather than made unreachable. The panel converged on the minimal fix; neither was executed as a counterfactual.

## Refutation verdict

The target does not survive as written. The contrary is only half-right: **58 is not a defensible set of 58 independent acceptance clauses**, but the observed count does not justify a cap, and “must resolve at derivation time” conflicts with derivation occurring before product edit. The primary defect is that a structural scanner promotes analysis-thread list items and citation-shaped tokens into a hard-gating acceptance surface.

## 1. The proposed volume cap has no valid baseline — `blocks-the-design`

**Evidence.** I re-counted every completed brief dated 2026-08-24 through 2026-08-27 (N=34). Current clause counts are 0–13, median 7; even after excluding seven zero-clause briefs, the median remains 7. Thus “9-to-13 norm” is not the corpus norm; it is the upper tail. More importantly, current completed state is not derivation output. Seventeen briefs preserve a numeric derivation count in `derived_reason`: median 8, maximum **72** on #3599, later normalized to 12. The claimed completed-corpus ceiling of 13 therefore cannot be used as an extractor ceiling.

I also measured thread size for the 17 numeric derivations plus #3794 (N=18), using issue-body plus comment characters and REST comment counts. Derived count versus comment count was Pearson 0.559 / Spearman 0.679; versus thread characters, Pearson 0.557 / Spearman 0.623. There is a moderate association, but thread length is not sufficient: #3599 produced 72 from 27 comments / 123,979 characters and #3794 produced 58 from 9 / 88,752, while #3806 produced 8 from 23 / 116,440 and #3611 produced 10 from 18 / 116,624. The n=1 trigger claim is not established, and the historical 72-output case shows #3794 is not unique.

**Concrete failure mode.** A numeric ceiling can refuse or truncate a legitimate complex contract based on a post-edited baseline, while an attacker can remain below the ceiling and still inject bad clauses. If excess volume falls back to a weaker surface, issue prose can deliberately trigger that fallback.

**Disposition consequence.** Reject the count-cap acceptance criterion as a correctness mechanism. A bounded-resource circuit breaker may still refuse and request normalization, but it must not truncate or decide which clauses are true.

## 2. Existing-path validation at derivation time is temporally unsound — `blocks-the-design`

**Evidence.** `applyClauseDerivationToPlan` records clauses “before product edit.” `walkAcceptanceClauses` performs the existing containment, scratch, existence, file-kind, and readability checks at verification time. There is no derivation-time normalizer beyond `looksLikeFilePath` / `extractPathTokens`; the quality pass checks statement provenance and ambiguity, not path semantics.

For #3794’s 58 bound paths, I classified the exact stored values: 21 line-range citations, 6 placeholders, 6 scratch paths, 3 directories, 20 other missing paths, and 2 existing files. The rerun at dispatch SHA `9e8396fcc18ee406ebb2991168b5e5690c728e97` reproduced **1 verified, 2 unverifiable, 55 failed**. Most failures are indeed unusable bindings, but a requirement that the artifact already exist at intake would also reject a legitimate clause for a new file—the normal pre-product-edit case.

**Concrete failure mode.** “Resolve now” prevents acceptance from naming artifacts the implementation is supposed to create. Conversely, accepting any existing path is not semantic validation: an existence-shaped clause can bind to an unrelated known file and pass.

**Disposition consequence.** Replace “resolves to a repository artifact at derivation” with validation appropriate to the phase: reject citation suffixes, placeholders, directories, foreign/scratch paths, and ambiguous first-path selection; permit a normalized repository-relative future-file path, then retain existence/content checks at done.

## 3. The 58-clause surface is analysis extraction, not unusually thorough acceptance — `blocks-the-design`

**Evidence.** The extractor is deterministic: it takes every list item under headings matching `Acceptance`, `Acceptance Criteria`, `Acceptance sketch`, or `Fix`, then labeled lines, with path-bearing bullets as fallback. Tests explicitly preserve later acceptance sections and comment-thread clauses. It does not classify obligation versus evidence, observation, caveat, or rejected option.

The live output demonstrates that distinction. Clauses begin with “Corroboration,” “Evidence,” “Cost,” “Sequencing with #3599,” “Correction that changes the cost analysis,” and “Method-reconciliation first.” Forty-one of 58 are marked ambiguous merely because their prose cites multiple paths. None of the 13 `plan.items` titles occurs exactly in the clause texts; token-overlap best matches are all below 0.16. Statement provenance does not rescue this: the rerun stamped 55 statement-provenance and 3 implementation-provenance clauses because provenance proves textual traceability, not acceptance authority.

**Concrete failure mode.** Untrusted issue text can add a `## Fix` heading and path-bearing bullets, causing diagnosis, quoted instructions, or hostile path tokens to become tracked gate input. A volume cap only changes how many such promotions occur; it does not prevent them.

**Disposition consequence.** Reframe the design around source authority and semantic selection: derive only from the bound acceptance contract (or explicit acceptance item fields), and represent citations separately from `artifact_path`. Do not describe the core defect as over-extraction by quantity.

## 4. `plan.items`, clause walk, and durability are distinct mechanisms — `sharpens-framing`

**Evidence.** The consumers are not alternatives today. `scope:complete` first runs `evaluateAcceptanceEvidenceGate(plan.items)`, requiring typed evidence or human disposition for non-terminal items, then separately runs `evaluateScopeCompleteAcceptanceWalk(plan)`. Failed clauses block unconditionally even when an executable acceptance command is green. Therefore “prefer `plan.items`” is an architectural change, not an existing fallback.

The durability claim also overstates the Git mechanism. I confirmed the brief is untracked, and `task check` is blocked by `verify:ac`. But `.githooks/pre-commit` runs encoding, forward coverage, and staged xBRIEF conformance—not full `task check` or `verify:ac`. The build contract reserves full check for the PR/merge chokepoint. The brief is not technically uncommittable; it is non-merge-ready and process-blocked. Its single-machine state is observed, but not caused by Git refusing a commit.

**Concrete failure mode.** Treating the surfaces as interchangeable can remove one gate while leaving the other hard failure in place, or silently weaken acceptance. Calling the artifact uncommittable can send the remedy toward commit plumbing instead of the derivation/done-gate composition.

**Disposition consequence.** Preserve the durability concern, but state it as “cannot reach a compliant PR/merge handoff.” Make the next design explicitly choose whether clauses are authoritative obligations, evidence pointers for items, or removable derived hints; then define one composition rule.

## Injection / swarm lens

Issue bodies and comments are untrusted and are deliberately retained across later sections. Today a heading plus bullets controls a tracked artifact that every done/check path reads. Provenance accepts textual presence, and ambiguity automatically chooses reading 0. This creates both injection and shared-work blockage: one careless or hostile thread can strand every worker whose repository-wide check sees the active brief. A hard maximum adds a second denial-of-service lever for legitimately long issues without fixing authority.

## Road not taken

Making missing or malformed `artifact_path` advisory in `verify:ac` would unstrand #3794, but I reject it as the primary remedy: `failed` is intentionally unconditional because a genuinely contradicted shipped-artifact claim must block. Move citation/authority filtering earlier and preserve done-time contradiction checks.

## Steelman and flip condition

The strongest case for a cap is operational safety: it bounds gate output and forces human normalization on pathological input. I would support that only as a refusal circuit breaker—no truncation, no silent fallback—and only after the contract identifies an authoritative source surface. I would reverse the rejection of a count-based correctness rule if a broader labeled corpus showed clause validity dropping at a stable threshold independent of source section and issue complexity; the present corpus does not.

## Comparator note — `footnote`

Re-reading local artifacts confirms #3796 = 8 clauses, #3831 = 9, and #3610 = 9. #3831 has 9 null `artifact_path` values, so a low count is not evidence of path quality. No #3819 xBRIEF is present in this checkout, so I could not independently verify that comparator. This note carries no disposition weight.

A careless or hostile body/comment can emit unbounded path-bearing bullets. Each unresolvable path is a hard `failed` row, so the brief cannot be committed — an availability hit on the story, not a reviewer problem. The same flood marks ceremony XL at count>6. A volume cap is itself a denial-of-service on a legitimate high-N checkbox issue; this brief shows the cap would not have kept a clause that mattered, because none of the 13 bound items were in the 58.

The walk's negated-existence + missing-file verify is an integrity hole on that untrusted text: clause 55 is critic prose, not a ship check, and it is the only green row. Any durability repair that treats `verified > 0` as sufficient must close that path first. That is a deterministic walk/stamp control, not attention.

I considered making missing `artifact_path` advisory. Rejected: it greens on the `git.ts` false verify (finding 3).

I considered "58 is derivation doing its job on a hard authz issue." Rejected: 0 overlap with the recut list; collectors never saw that list (finding 2).

That would flip if the 58 overlapped the bound 13 and walked green against shipped files. Measured: overlap 0; 55 failed; the one verify is a missing bare filename plus "does not exist" in critic prose. Does not flip.

The strongest case for a cap: 75/72/58 already happened, so a fuse is cheaper than another stranded brief. That would flip if thread length predicted count and the bound criteria sat in the first N derived rows. Measured: r=0.23 on comments; the 13 are not in the 58. Does not flip.

Would a cap have suppressed a clause that mattered on #3794? No. The clauses that mattered were never derived.

Corpus attribution across all 110 derived-clause briefs:

|---|---|---|---|
| primary extractors (1-3) produced >= 1 item | 44 | 6.2 | **13** |
| fell through to `collectPathBearingLines` | 66 | 5.4 | **58** |

## blocks-the-design 3 -- `verify:ac` is a file-content read oracle driven by untrusted issue prose, and no volume cap touches it

Injection / swarm lens. Derivation consumes untrusted issue-thread text and writes it into an artifact that gates work; `verify:ac` then executes filesystem reads against strings from that text.

**Evidence, the chain end to end:**

1. `narratives.Overview` on the #3794 brief is **84,535 characters** of verbatim issue-thread text -- the whole discussion. `collectTaskStatementFromPlan` (`clause-derivation.ts:92-128`) pushes every narrative value into the derivation input, including an unbounded loop over `Object.entries(narratives)`.
2. Branch 4 lifts any bullet with a path token. `artifact_path` comes from `extractPathTokens` on that untrusted line.
3. `walkOne` (`clauses.ts:388-512`) does `resolve(projectRoot, artifactPath)`, checks containment against project root only, then -- when `extractExpectedTokens` finds quoted strings in the clause text -- **`readFileSync(abs, 'utf8')` and `body.includes(token)`**, reporting `expected token(s) missing from <path>: <token>` on miss and `tokens present in shipped artifact <path>` on hit.

`extractExpectedTokens` (`clauses.ts:367-386`) takes its tokens from the same untrusted clause text. **15 of the 58 clauses on this brief already carry quoted expected-tokens.** The paths derivation actually emitted include `C:/Repos/deft/directive/.git` and `<root>/.deft/authz/audit.jsonl` -- both from thread prose, neither authored as an acceptance path.

So a bullet in any issue comment of the form ``- The token "ghp_" exists in `.git/config` `` yields a clause whose walk reads `.git/config` and reports a one-bit answer about its contents in the `verify:ac` output, which is printed to console, captured in run summaries, and pasted into handbacks. Containment stops traversal outside the root; it does not stop reads of `.git/config`, `.env`, `xbrief/`, or `.deft/authz/audit.jsonl`, all of which are inside the root. `EXISTENCE_CLAIM` and `NEGATED_EXISTENCE` give the same primitive for existence rather than content.

**Failure mode:** an in-root secret-bearing file is probed one substring at a time by anyone who can comment on an issue that later gets ingested. Repeated across clauses this is an enumeration channel, and the report text carries the answer out to wherever the walk output goes.

**Disposition consequence:** this is the strongest reason the volume axis is wrong, and it survives every remedy in the body. **One crafted bullet is under any cap.** A cap at 13, at 20, at 5 changes nothing. The controls that would bind are an allowlist on `artifact_path` shape at derivation, refusing dotfile and VCS-metadata directories in `walkOne`, and not sourcing `extractExpectedTokens` from untrusted clause text -- none of which is in the body's remedy list or acceptance set. I am not resting this on review attention: the deterministic control is a path predicate in `looksLikeFilePath` plus a deny segment set in `walkOne` alongside the existing `SCRATCH_SEGMENTS`, both of which are single-function changes at known lines.

This is not the "cap creates a DoS on legitimate complex issues" risk the envelope asked about, which is real but bounded and is the author's own trade-off to make.
